title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: From Word Counts to Large Language Models
subtitle: with a case study on JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, Vanguard and Citadel
abstract: Financial text is hard for general sentiment tools: domain words have special meanings, bad news is often just a number going down, and a headline that mentions a bank is often not about the bank. We compare the model families covered in the Language Technologies course on the same financial sentiment task: a finance lexicon, TF-IDF with logistic regression, GloVe and our own finance embeddings with an FFNN, a CNN and a BiLSTM, fine-tuned BERT and FinBERT, and Qwen2.5 LLMs prompted with zero or six examples. All models are evaluated on the Financial PhraseBank with five runs and 95% confidence intervals, and on financial tweets that none of them was trained on.

Fine-tuned BERT is the best model on PhraseBank (83.5 macro-F1), but Qwen2.5-1.5B prompted with six examples comes within four points without any training and is the most robust model on tweets. Domain-specific pre-training does not help on PhraseBank, but FinBERT beats BERT by up to 12 points on tweets. A case study on JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, Vanguard and Citadel shows that only 42% of the headlines that mention these firms are actually about them, so sentence-level sentiment is a poor proxy for sentiment towards a firm.
keywords: financial sentiment analysis, Financial PhraseBank, word embeddings, FinBERT, large language models, prompting
